Chapter Two: The Art of Answering Impossible Questions
Working in a bookshop? It pretty much means becoming an expert at tackling the impossible. Every single day, you’ll face questions that don’t seem to have an answer—at least, not one that actually makes sense in the world of books. But somehow, bookshop staff always find a way to respond. How do they do it? With a little creativity, a lot of empathy, and—maybe most important of all—a big helping of humor.
Let me paint you a picture. One morning, a customer strides in, radiating urgency. “Do you have that book? The one everyone’s talking about?” Ever heard that before? If you’ve worked in a bookshop, you probably have. The staff member, totally unfazed by the vagueness, asks for more details. But the customer just frowns, as if the answer should be obvious. “You know, the one with the thing on the cover.”
After a few minutes of back-and-forth, it becomes clear—they have no clue who wrote the book, what it’s called, or even what it’s about. All they remember is that it was mentioned on the radio… or was it television? Sometime in the last month, maybe. The staff, undeterred, start rattling off recent bestsellers, just hoping something will click. Sometimes, this rabbit-hole approach actually works. Other times, the customer walks out, still chasing that elusive book.
But that’s just the beginning. Some questions show a pretty hilarious misunderstanding of, well, how books even work. Someone once asked if the shop carried “books that can be read backwards,” convinced such a thing had to exist. Another person wanted a book with all the answers—as if one volume could possibly contain humanity’s entire knowledge base. The staff, always patient, explained that encyclopedias come close, but even they can’t do it all.
And then there are the truly bizarre, oddly specific requests. Like the customer who wanted a book “about penguins, but only the ones living in zoos.” Not all penguins—just the captive ones. When told that most penguin books cover the species as a whole, they firmly insisted there must be a book out there all about zoo penguins. The staff promised to look into it… knowing full well that book probably doesn’t exist.
Some requests feel like they’re from another planet. One person asked for “the book that explains why my cat hates me.” Another wanted a manual on “how to become invisible”—and yes, they were completely serious. The staff, caught between wanting to help and not wanting to laugh, did their best to offer some suggestions, even if nothing was quite what the customer had in mind.
Through all of this, you quickly learn to approach every question with an open mind. Most people don’t realize just how tough it can be to track down a book based on the vaguest clues, or how often these impossible questions pop up each day. But after a while, it becomes second nature. The staff develop what you might call a sixth sense—piecing together tiny scraps of information and turning them into something useful.
Here’s what really stands out: the sheer creativity it takes to answer these questions. It’s not just about knowing what’s on the shelves or recommending a good read. It’s about understanding what the customer is truly looking for—even when they can’t put it into words. Sometimes, it means reading between the lines, catching a stray word or a half-remembered detail, and using that as your starting point.
So, next time you find yourself asking for “that book with the thing on the cover,” remember: behind the counter is someone who’s mastered the art of the impossible—and is always ready for the next challenge.
